title: Sealing, stain protection and cure times
audience: Stone and terrazzo restoration technicians who apply sealers and impregnators and who hand the finished surface back to the client
learningOutcomes: Explain what a sealer or impregnator does and what it does not do
Choose a sealer by stone type, finish and traffic using the manufacturer's data
Apply thin, even coats and respect the stated dwell, buffing and cure times
Give the client written care and re-seal instructions at handover
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Queensland, Chemical reaction exposes worker to toxic gas (no date on page; incident dated March 2022).

instruction.heading: What sealing does and does not do
instruction.body: A sealer or impregnator reduces the absorption of the stone, which makes it slower to stain and easier to clean. It does not make a worn or damaged surface sound, it does not fill cracks, and it does not hide defects. A sealer applied over a surface with dirt, slurry or residue traps the contamination and can affect the finish and the cure. For this reason, sealing comes after the surface is clean, dry to the product's requirement and confirmed as the right stone with a passing test patch (“Pre-work surface assessment and test patches”). Choose the sealer from the manufacturer's data for the stone type, the finish and the traffic it will carry. Some sealers change the sheen, so the test patch should show the finish as well as the protection.

instruction.heading: Application and cure
instruction.body: Follow the product's instructions for the number of coats, the coverage rate, the dwell time, any buffing and the cure time. Apply thin, even coats. A thick coat does not seal faster, and it can trap solvent, leave a tacky film or leave a line. Remove the excess before it sets, as the product directs. Keep the area ventilated, because many sealers have solvents that the SDS will describe (“Chemicals for stone: acid etches, cleaners and sealers”). Keep the area closed to traffic for the cure time. Temperature, humidity and moisture in the stone change the cure, so read the product data for the conditions on the day and record them. If the surface is not dry when the product requires it, stop and wait.

instruction.heading: Handover and client care
instruction.body: At handover, tell the client in writing the cure time, the time before the area can be walked on and the time before it can be washed. Give the client the list of cleaning products that the manufacturer approves, and the products to avoid, including acidic cleaners, abrasive pads and solvent cleaners where the product data says they are unsuitable. Explain when the surface should be re-sealed, as the product data sets. Record the product name, batch, application date and coat count. Where a sealer change or a second product is planned, check the compatibility in the product data before application. The care note is part of the job, and it protects the finish that the client paid for.

procedure: Confirm that the surface is clean, dry to the product requirement and passed by the test patch.
Read the SDS and the product data sheet for the sealer, and check its suitability for the stone and the finish.
Ventilate the area and set up the PPE listed in the SDS.
Apply a thin, even coat using the method and tools the product directs.
Remove the excess before it sets, as the product directs.
Apply the next coat only after the stated interval, and do not exceed the stated coat count.
Close the area for the cure time, and record the conditions on the day.
Give the client written care instructions and the re-seal interval, and file the product record.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a freshly honed granite kitchen bench to be sealed on the same afternoon, and wants to use the kitchen that evening. The bench is dry on the surface but the slurry residue is still in the edges.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the technician do about the sealing, the timing and the client's request?
workedExamples.reasoning: The residue must be removed and the surface must be dry to the product requirement before sealing. The technician cleans the edges with the wet method, confirms the dryness, and applies thin coats as the product directs. The technician explains that the cure time will not allow same-evening use of the bench, and writes the cure time and the approved cleaners on the care note. The technician does not promise a shorter cure than the product data states.

equipmentAndPpe: Sealer or impregnator approved for the stone and the finish, with its SDS and data sheet
Applicator pads or brushes as the product directs
Ventilation or extraction suited to the product
PPE listed in the SDS for the product

commonErrors.error: Sealing over dirt, slurry or residue.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean and confirm dryness first. Sealing traps contamination.

commonErrors.error: Applying thick coats to speed up the job.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply thin, even coats and remove the excess as the product directs.

commonErrors.error: Telling the client that any cleaner is fine after sealing.
commonErrors.prevention: Give the client the manufacturer's approved cleaning list and the products to avoid.
Check compatibility in the product data before any second product is used.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Sealers and solvents carry hazards that are described in the SDS. Follow the SDS.
Sealing work does not grant any licence, certificate or authority to carry out other stone restoration work.
Stop-work rule: stop if the surface is not dry to the product requirement, if the test patch has not been passed, or if the sealer is not approved for the stone and finish.

qualityStandard: The surface is clean, dry to the product requirement and passed by the test patch before sealing.
The coat count, coverage, dwell and cure times follow the product data.
The client receives written care and re-seal instructions at handover.
The product, batch and application record are on file.
documentationEvidence: Product name, batch number and SDS reference
Coat count, coverage rate, dwell and cure times, and conditions on the day
Client care note, with approved cleaners, avoid-list and re-seal interval
summary: A sealer reduces absorption and staining; it does not repair damage or hide defects.
Seal only clean, dry, tested surfaces.
Apply thin, even coats and respect the stated cure time.
Give the client written care instructions and the approved cleaners.
Record the product, batch, coats and cure conditions.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: WorkSafe Queensland, Chemical reaction exposes worker to toxic gas (no date on page; incident dated March 2022).

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a sealer do?
options: It reduces absorption and staining
It hides all the damage in the stone
It makes a worn stone sound again
It replaces the need for polishing

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is sealing over slurry residue a mistake?
options: It is faster to do it that way on the job site today
It can trap the residue and affect the finish and the cure
It makes the stone harder to work and to polish later on
It removes the dust from the surface before the seal

knowledgeChecks.question: Which approach to coats is correct?
options: Thick coats for speed and fewer passes
Random coats across the surface at any time
Thin, even coats following the product data
One coat in every case, whatever the product

knowledgeChecks.question: What should the client receive at handover?
options: Nothing at all for the client to keep at home today
A licence for the surface, the stone and the seal
A verbal instruction only, given at the door of the house
Written cure time, approved cleaners and the re-seal interval

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks to use a harsh cleaner on the sealed surface. What should the technician say?
options: Only the cleaners listed in the product care guidance may be used
Yes, any cleaner is fine on the stone surface at all times
Use vinegar at all times on the sealed stone surface and the floor
Ask a neighbour who knows stone to advise on the cleaner
